points.title: Why hex matches binary
points.must: 16 = 2⁴: a nibble has 16 patterns and hex has 16 digits, so one hex digit = exactly 4 bits; each hex place covers its own 4 bits; denary has no such link.
points.model: 16 = 2⁴, so 4 bits give 16 patterns (0000–1111 = 0–15) and hex has 16 digits (0–F): one hex digit = exactly one nibble. Hex place values 16 = 2⁴, 256 = 2⁸, so each hex digit covers its own block of 4 bits. 10 is not a power of 2, so denary digits do not match groups of bits.

points.title: Nibble
points.must: Definition of nibble: 4 bits, 16 values, one hex digit.
points.model: Nibble — a group of 4 bits, half a byte; 16 values (0–15), one hexadecimal digit.

points.title: Hex digit table
points.must: The table 0–F with denary 0–15 and 4-bit binary 0000–1111.

points.title: Binary → hex
points.must: Group into nibbles from the RIGHT, pad the left group with leading zeros, convert each nibble; why from the right; example.
points.model: Split into groups of 4 bits from the right, add leading 0s to the left group, change each nibble to one hex digit. 11010011 → 1101 0011 → D3. 101101 → 0010 1101 → 2D (grouping from the left gives a wrong answer).

points.title: Hex → binary
points.must: Each hex digit becomes exactly 4 bits (keep zeros inside groups); example.
points.model: Write each hex digit as exactly 4 bits. 5C → 0101 1100 = 01011100. A5 → 1010 0101 (not 1010101).

points.title: Hex → denary
points.must: Place values 1, 16, 256; letters to values; multiply and add; examples (7A = 122; 1F4 = 500).

points.title: Denary → hex
points.must: Divide by 16: quotient and remainder (repeat for large numbers, read bottom up), or go via binary; example.
points.model: Divide by 16: quotient = left digit, remainder = right digit (10–15 → A–F). 245 = 15×16 + 5 → F5. Large: 500 ÷16 = 31 r 4; 31 ÷16 = 1 r 15 (F); 1 ÷16 = 0 r 1 → 1F4. Or denary → binary → hex: 245 = 1111 0101 = F5.

points.title: Hex is only for people
points.must: The computer stores and processes binary; hex is a shorthand to display binary for humans; it does not save memory or make the computer faster.
points.model: The computer stores and processes only binary. Hexadecimal is a way for people to write/display binary values. It does not use less memory and does not make processing faster.

points.title: Advantages of hexadecimal (explained)
points.must: Each advantage with its reason: shorter (1 digit = 4 bits, byte = 2 digits); easier to read/remember/compare; fewer errors when copying; easy conversion to binary digit by digit (unlike denary); lines up with bytes and memory.
points.model: Shorter — one hex digit replaces 4 bits, a byte is 2 digits instead of 8. Easier for people to read, remember and compare (FF vs F0). Fewer errors when copying/typing because there are fewer digits. Easy to convert to/from binary digit by digit, unlike denary, so the bits can still be seen. Lines up with bytes: 2 digits = 1 byte.

points.title: RGB colour codes
points.must: Definition: #RRGGBB, three bytes red/green/blue 0–255; worked example #1E90C8 = (30, 144, 200).
points.model: RGB colour code — three bytes for red, green, blue (0–255 each), written #RRGGBB. #000000 black, #FFFFFF white, #FF0000 red. #1E90C8: 1E = 30, 90 = 144, C8 = 200 → RGB(30, 144, 200).

points.title: Memory addresses and memory dumps
points.must: Definition of memory address; dumps show addresses and bytes in hex; text can be read (48 65 6C 6C 6F = Hello).
points.model: Memory address — a number identifying one byte location in memory, shown in hex (0x7FFE0010). A memory dump lists addresses and bytes in hex, 2 digits per byte: 48 65 6C 6C 6F = ASCII 'Hello'.

points.title: MAC addresses and other uses
points.must: MAC address = 48 bits = 6 bytes = 12 hex digits (first 3 bytes = manufacturer); IPv6, Unicode, error codes, machine code / assembly.
points.model: MAC address — 48-bit hardware address of a network card, 6 pairs of hex digits: 3C-A8-2A-F0-11-6B. Other uses: IPv6 (128 bits, 8 groups of 4 hex digits), Unicode (U+0416), error codes (0x0000007B), machine code and assembly.

points.title: Hex vs denary vs binary
points.must: Comparison: digits per byte (8 / up to 3 / always 2), readability, ease of conversion to binary, lining up with bytes.
points.model: One byte: binary 8 digits (hard to read), denary up to 3 digits (no link to bits, needs arithmetic), hex always 2 digits (easy to read and converts digit by digit to binary).

points.title: Prefixes for hexadecimal
points.must: 0x, #, h suffix, subscript 16 — and why they are needed.
points.model: Hex prefixes: 0x1F (programming), #1F4FD8 (colours), 1Fh, 1F₁₆. Without a prefix '10' could be ten, two or sixteen.

points.title: Common mistakes
points.must: Group from the right; letters A–F not two digits; keep 4 bits per digit; place values 16 and 256; hex is not stored; colour pairs RR GG BB; MAC = 6 bytes.
points.model: Group nibbles from the right. Write 10–15 as A–F. Each hex digit = exactly 4 bits. Hex place values are 16, 256 (not 10, 100). The computer stores binary, not hex. Colour code pairs = RR GG BB. MAC address = 6 bytes = 48 bits.
